findings.title: No runnable path reproduces any reported table or figure
findings.claim: The constructed datasets, trained models/experiments, and the ESCI (`zero_shot`) construction directory are all git-excluded; the surviving preprocessing is Jupyter-notebook-only with hardcoded absolute paths (e.g. `scripts/unified_user/seq_user_pipline.sh` hardcodes `/home/jupyter/unity_jointly_rec_and_search/...`), and the primary Lowe's dataset is private. No committed config/seed maps a run to any table cell.
findings.concern: Every quantitative artefact in the paper (Tables 3–5, Figs 3–4, the abstract's 45% claim) traces to data that is private or git-excluded and to preprocessing that cannot be executed as shipped, so none of the reported numbers can be independently reproduced or verified from this repository.
findings.resolution: Provide the ESCI construction as runnable scripts with relative/parameterised paths, ship (or give a fetch script for) the constructed ESCI splits and qrels, and add exact commands + configs that map to each table; for Lowe's, state clearly that only ESCI is reproducible.

findings.title: No significance-test code for the pervasive p<0.01 markers
findings.quote: We use two-tailed paired t-test with Bonferroni correction to identify statistically significant improvements (p_value < 0.01).
findings.claim: Tables 3, 4 and 5 annotate results with significance superscripts (△ = better than all task-specific baselines, ▲ = better than all baselines, ▽ = worse than UIA), all at p<0.01 via a paired t-test with Bonferroni correction; a whole-repo search (py/ipynb/sh) finds no t-test, no Bonferroni/multiple-comparison correction, and no `scipy.stats`/`statsmodels` usage (the only `scipy` import is `scipy.sparse` in `trainer/pretrain_cf.ipynb`).
findings.concern: The paper's central empirical claim — 'significant improvements compared to all baselines' — rests on significance markers that no artefact in the repo computes, so the significance testing cannot be checked or reproduced.
findings.resolution: Release the script that computes the per-query paired t-tests and Bonferroni correction, including which per-query metric arrays and how many comparisons feed the correction.

findings.title: Author-implemented JSR/SRJGraph (and all baselines) absent from repo
findings.quote: We use the provided public code to implement BM25, NCF, DPR, ANCE, RocketQA, SASRec++ and BERT4Rec. We implemented JSR and SRJGraph which don't have public implementations.
findings.claim: The paper reports JSR, JSR+BERT4Rec++, and SRJGraph as joint-training baselines that UIA must beat, and states the authors implemented JSR and SRJGraph themselves; a whole-repo search (py/ipynb/sh) finds no JSR, SRJGraph, NCF, BERT4Rec, or RocketQA code (only `modeling/sas_rec.py` and the dual-encoders exist).
findings.concern: The paper's core comparative claim (UIA significantly outperforms all baselines, including joint-training JSR/SRJGraph) cannot be reproduced because the baselines it is compared against — including the two the authors say they implemented — are not in the repository.
findings.resolution: Release the JSR and SRJGraph implementations (and the config/adaptations for NCF, BERT4Rec++, RocketQA) used to produce Tables 3–4.

findings.title: No dependency spec and no reproduction instructions
findings.claim: The only top-level README is the abstract plus an architecture image — no install steps, no dataset download, no run commands, no results table. No dependency specification (requirements.txt / environment.yml / setup.py / pyproject / Pipfile / conda.yaml) exists anywhere in the repo, though the code imports pinned-version-sensitive libraries (torch, faiss, transformers, ujson).
findings.concern: Without a dependency spec or any documented command sequence, the environment cannot be rebuilt and the pipeline cannot be run end-to-end, blocking reproduction independently of the data-availability gap.
findings.resolution: Add a requirements.txt/environment.yml with pinned versions and a README section giving the exact preprocess→train→index→retrieve→evaluate commands for the public ESCI dataset.

findings.title: Two committed scripts do not compile (dead/unused)
findings.quote: qid, pid, rank, score = int(array[0]), int(array[1]), int(array[2]) float(array[3])
findings.claim: `evaluation/metrics.py:35` is missing a comma (`int(array[2]) float(array[3])`) and raises SyntaxError; `preprocess/unified_user/divide_user_by_groups.py:120` has raw shell commands pasted into a `.py` file. `check_syntax.py` compiles 80 files and reports exactly these two failures. Neither file is imported anywhere (metrics.py is not in `evaluation/__init__.py`; the main evaluator is the separate `retrieval_evaluator.py`).
findings.concern: Both files are broken but unused, so they do not affect the pipeline; they are committed dead code that a reviewer might mistake for live evaluation/preprocessing utilities.
findings.resolution: Delete the dead files or fix them, and confirm the live evaluation path is `evaluation/retrieval_evaluator.py`.

findings.title: RerankingEvaluator calls write_rankdata but its import is commented out
findings.quote:
if output_rerank_path is not None:
    write_rankdata(qid_to_rankdata, output_rerank_path)
findings.claim: `reranking_evaluator.py:85` calls `write_rankdata`, but its only import is commented out at line 13 (`#from utils import write_rankdata`), so the name is undefined → NameError whenever `output_rerank_path` is set. (Separately, the `write_rankdata` in `evaluation/utils.py` has an orphaned `self.qid_to_relevant_data`/`qrel_path` block at lines 162–178 that would also NameError if that copy were called.)
findings.concern: The cross-encoder reranking evaluation path is broken; it is auxiliary (the paper's headline results are pure dense retrieval via `retrieval_evaluator.py`), so impact is limited, but any reranking eval crashes.
findings.resolution: Uncomment/fix the `write_rankdata` import in `reranking_evaluator.py` and remove the dangling block in `utils.py`; confirm reranking was not used for any reported table.

findings.title: APN position-embedding branch references undefined `config`
findings.claim: In `UserSeqEncoder.__init__`, the position-embedding branch passes `config`, which is never defined in that scope (only `model_args`/`backbone_args` exist) → NameError. The same pattern appears in `user_seq_merge_encoder.py:190` and `user_seq_self_encoder.py:174`. It is gated by `apply_position_embedding`, whose default is `False` (`user_argument.py:8`) and which no shell script sets true, so the branch is latent.
findings.concern: Enabling positional embeddings in the personalization network — a documented model option — crashes on construction, so that configuration was never actually runnable.
findings.resolution: Change `PositionEmbedding(config)` to `PositionEmbedding(model_args)` in the three encoders, or confirm the reported models never used positional embeddings.

findings.title: Main code directory's README documents a different paper (CL-DRD)
findings.quote:
# Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation (CL-DRD)
Hansi Zeng, Hamed Zamani, Vishwa, Vinay

This repo provides code, trained models for our SIGIR'22 paper: [Curriculum Learning for Dense Retrieval Distillation](https://hansizeng.github.io/).
findings.claim: The directory that holds all UIA model/training/eval code (`kgc-dr/`) ships a README for the authors' earlier SIGIR'22 CL-DRD paper, with CL-DRD inference commands and MS MARCO numbers, not UIA. The code itself is genuinely the UIA extension (bi-encoder + APN + unified training), so this is a documentation mismatch, not wrong code.
findings.concern: A reader following `kgc-dr/README.md` gets instructions and a results table for a different paper, which misdirects reproduction and obscures which scripts correspond to UIA's Tables 3–5.
findings.resolution: Replace `kgc-dr/README.md` with UIA-specific documentation (or point it at the top-level README) and remove the stale CL-DRD instructions.

findings.title: ESCI query-by-example / complementary pairs use a random pair split
findings.quote: Since there is no user identifiers or timestamp available in the Amazon ESCI dataset, we randomly select 80% of requests (e.g., query text or query item) for training, 10% for validation, and the remaining 10% for testing.
findings.claim: For the ESCI Query-by-Example and Complementary tasks, requests are item→item pairs {(i1,i2)}; a random 80/10/10 split over these pairs can place the same anchor item i1 (and target item i2) in both train and test, so the model can be tested on anchors whose relations it saw during training. The construction/split lives in git-excluded notebooks (`preprocess/unified_user/zero_shot/*.ipynb`), so I could not verify from code whether any entity-disjoint control is applied.
findings.concern: A random pair split on item→item tasks risks per-item memorisation rather than generalisation, which could inflate the ESCI QBE/CIR numbers; whether it materially does cannot be determined from the shipped code (data and split notebooks are absent/uninspectable).
findings.resolution: Authors: report anchor/target overlap between train and test for the ESCI QBE and CIR splits, and/or add an entity-disjoint split as a control; release the split script so overlap can be measured.
